Architecture Diagram

The solution is a single ASP.NET Web Forms application with a catalog service layer and Entity Framework persistence. It can use mock data locally or connect to SQL Server, with optional Azure integrations for image storage, identity, and telemetry.

Data Storage & External Services

The application uses SQL Server through Entity Framework when mock mode is disabled; the Compose configuration provides a SQL Server development container. Mock mode instead keeps catalog items in an in-memory list. Azure Blob Storage is an optional image backend, Azure Active Directory is an optional OpenID Connect provider, and Application Insights is an optional telemetry sink.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • The application is a single deployable Web Forms project rather than a set of independently deployed business services.
  • ICatalogService and IImageService separate page code from SQL/mock catalog and local/Azure image implementations.
  • Autofac modules select implementations from externalized feature settings; EF6 is the persistence ORM.

DTOs & Contracts

There are no dedicated immutable API DTOs. Web Forms and the catalog service use the mutable CatalogItem, CatalogBrand, and CatalogType model classes directly; PaginatedItemsViewModel carries page metadata and results. The ASMX upload method returns an anonymous JSON object containing an image name and URL, serialized with JavaScriptSerializer. No OpenAPI, protobuf, or GraphQL contract was found.

Communication Patterns

Page code synchronously calls ICatalogService; the SQL implementation uses Entity Framework 6 and CatalogDBContext, while mock mode uses an in-memory service. Image handling calls either the mock image service or Azure Blob Storage. There is no active message-broker flow, service discovery, API gateway, retry policy, circuit breaker, or explicit timeout policy in the application code.

Azure AD OpenID Connect can be enabled by configuration. When it is disabled, the OWIN pipeline uses the application's custom middleware; no role-based authorization policy was identified. The development container publishes HTTP port 80 to host port 5114, and no application-level TLS termination is configured in the assessed workspace. The Compose file defines a SQL health check but no explicit application startup dependency on that health check.

Core Business Workflows

The application supports browsing and maintaining a product catalog. Catalog items are categorized by brand and type, with pricing, inventory thresholds, and optional product images.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
CatalogItemCatalog ManagementProduct displayed and maintained in the catalogBelongs to one brand and one type
CatalogBrandCatalog ManagementBrand classification for productsHas zero or more catalog items
CatalogTypeCatalog ManagementType/category classification for productsHas zero or more catalog items

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
eShopModernizedWebFormsCatalog ManagementCatalogItem, CatalogBrand, CatalogTypeSQL Server or mock catalog; optional Azure Blob Storage for images

The application is the source of truth for catalog records. It has no separate business services or cross-context entity references.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Browse the Catalog

  1. A visitor opens the default route or a page/size route.
  2. The page asks the catalog service for the selected page of items.
  3. SQL mode reads catalog items and their brand/type through EF6; mock mode uses its in-memory catalog.
  4. The page builds image URLs and renders a paginated catalog.

Workflow 2: Create or Update a Catalog Item

  1. The user opens the Create or Edit page. When Azure AD is enabled, the page challenges unauthenticated users through OpenID Connect.
  2. The user supplies item details and may stage an image through the ASMX upload method.
  3. Form validators check required name and numeric price/stock ranges.
  4. The catalog service creates or updates the item in SQL Server or the mock catalog.
  5. If an image was staged and Azure storage is enabled, the image service promotes the temporary blob to the item location.
  6. The page redirects to the catalog.

Workflow 3: Delete a Catalog Item

  1. The user opens the item-specific delete page and sees the catalog item.
  2. The user confirms deletion.
  3. The catalog service removes the item from SQL Server or the mock catalog, and the page redirects to the catalog.

Workflow 4: Upload an Item Image

  1. The browser submits an image and item identifier to PicUploader.
  2. The endpoint decodes the upload and permits JPEG, PNG, or GIF image formats.
  3. Azure mode writes the image to a temporary Blob Storage name; mock mode returns its default or existing local image URL.
  4. The upload response returns the image name and URL as JSON.

Cross-Service Data Flows

There is no multi-service business aggregation. The application reads and writes catalog data directly through EF6 to its SQL database. Image bytes flow separately to Azure Blob Storage when enabled; otherwise the mock image service is selected. Azure AD and Application Insights are optional infrastructure integrations and do not provide catalog data.

Business Workflow Sequence

sequenceDiagram participant User as "Catalog Manager" participant Page as "Create Catalog Page" participant Service as "Catalog Service" participant DB as "SQL Server" participant Image as "Image Service" participant Blob as "Azure Blob Storage" User->>Page: Submit catalog item Page->>Page: Validate required name and numeric ranges Page->>Service: Create catalog item alt SQL persistence enabled Service->>DB: Insert catalog record DB-->>Service: Saved catalog item else Mock data enabled Service->>Service: Add item to in-memory list end opt Image was uploaded and Azure storage is enabled Page->>Image: Promote temporary image Image->>Blob: Copy image to item location Blob-->>Image: Copy completed end Service-->>Page: Create completed Page-->>User: Redirect to catalog

Business Rules & Decision Logic

  • Catalog item creation requires a name; price is constrained to nonnegative currency values with at most two decimal places.
  • Available stock, restock threshold, and maximum stock are constrained to the configured nonnegative range.
  • Each item must reference an existing brand and type through required foreign keys.
  • Catalog item identifiers are allocated by the HiLo sequence generator in SQL mode; mock mode increments the largest current item identifier.
  • Image upload accepts only decoded JPEG, PNG, or GIF formats.
  • Catalog data is seeded from preconfigured data by default; optional customization mode loads CSV and image data from the Setup directory.
  • No order, checkout, payment, or customer-management workflow was found.

Version & Compatibility Risks

The application targets .NET Framework 4.7.2 and depends on EF6, OWIN, older IdentityModel packages, and a beta generation of configuration builders. The CVE scan matched the declared log4net 2.0.10 and Microsoft IdentityModel token packages to medium-severity advisories. The dependency-list CLI could not evaluate the legacy project because Microsoft.WebApplication.targets is absent, so the vulnerability scan used direct package-manifest entries rather than a resolved transitive tree.

Notable Observations

  • packages.config contains 147 entries; the project has no separate test project or test-scoped package set.
  • The project declares Redis and Azure Service Bus packages, but no active cache or message-bus flow was identified in the application source/configuration.
  • Application Insights, Azure Storage, Azure AD, and Key Vault integrations are optional and controlled by configuration.

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

The application models a small product catalog with three EF6 entities stored in SQL Server. Entity Framework 6.3.0 provides persistence; an in-memory catalog service is available for mock mode.

The initializer creates the database if absent, runs SQL sequence scripts, and seeds configured or preconfigured catalog data. Optional customization data is read from CSV files and product-image archives.

Caching Strategy

No application-level catalog cache was identified. Redis client and session-state packages are present, but the custom Redis session configuration in Web.config is commented out. Mock mode stores a mutable list in process rather than using a cache provider.

Data Ownership Boundaries

The Web Forms application is the only service accessing the catalog database; no cross-service database access, CQRS split, or event-based data synchronization was found. The SQL database is a shared persistence dependency for the application, and image storage is a separate optional Azure Blob integration. With mock mode enabled, the catalog is held in an in-memory service instead.
